name: Erik Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing. This is confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day at the contact centre.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I open the complaints queue and take the calls that bounced twice before reaching us. I lead a small team, and I am good at finding the missed line in an account history. I have a two-year college diploma, but most of what makes me useful came from years beside more experienced agents.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is going on outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27 and rent on my own, with no children. My pay is ordinary for this job, and I have about four months of expenses saved. There are a few other centres around, although I would rather keep the work and people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the machines can write a short note, but the desk still needs someone who understands a complaint. I would remind my team to check every note before a customer sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be comfortable if work carried on much the same. I have four months put aside and my rent is manageable, though I would not spend that money to chase a new gadget. I have never used an AI tool and do not see a reason to start for a tiny saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my complaints queue and check the summaries the company gives me. I would ask a colleague to show me where errors usually turn up, then carry on with the same shifts. In the first year, I would keep adding a little to the reserve rather than buying another device.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job in this picture. The thing that bothers me is being told every small change is a grand new era.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error would you check for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missing promise about a refund. A customer remembers what we said, and I am the person they call when the record says something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep adding to savings when you already have four months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months is a cushion, not a plan to stop working. I grew up hearing that you fix the roof before the rain, and a bit more put aside lets me sleep.

say: I would say **complaint work** still needs a person who knows the history.
I would tell my team to check each **summary** before sending it.
think: I feel my **job** is secure in this picture.
I would rather protect my **reserve** than chase a small gadget gain.
do: Keep handling the **complaints queue** and check machine notes.
Ask a **colleague** where missing refund promises show up.
Add a little to my **reserve** during the first year.
feel: **Irritated** by inflated talk about small changes.
S0.quote: A customer remembers what we said, and I am the person they call when the record says something else.
fieldNote: He trusts years of **case experience** more than a new tool.
His four-month **reserve** supports a calm mood.
He accepts checking summaries without adopting **AI** himself.

steps.text: Keep handling complaints and check each machine case summary
Add a little from each pay to his four-month reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor that a quick answer is not the same as a correct one. I would ask the manager to count reopened complaints before replacing any more agents with a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I fear the easy calls will go first and then management will decide one lead can cover two teams. I am among the best at this desk, but that does not set the staffing budget. There are some other centres nearby, yet they may all make the same cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep a written record of cases the answer system gets wrong and bring it to our monthly meeting. I would sit in on a demonstration if required, but I would not pay for a course I do not trust. In the first year of these changes, if my hours fall I would apply to the other centres while keeping this wage as long as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because this reaches the work I do on a screen every day. I can defend good service, but I cannot make a manager keep a seat open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new system well enough to check it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the parts I must check at work, yes. I will not pretend I enjoy it or spend my evenings mastering a tool that may remove my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the monthly record need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The original answer, the reopened call and the time spent putting it right. If that cost is real, the manager should see it next to the promised savings.

say: I would ask managers to count **reopened complaints** before cutting seats.
I would say a quick answer can still be **wrong**.
think: I fear one lead may cover **two teams**.
I cannot rely on nearby centres if they face the **same cuts**.
do: Record wrong **answers** and reopened calls this month.
Apply to nearby **centres** if my hours fall.
feel: **Frustrated** that service evidence may lose to budgets.
S1.quote: I can defend good service, but I cannot make a manager keep a seat open.
fieldNote: His first response is to document **customer harm**, not buy training.
He will learn only the checks his current **job requires**.
Local alternatives exist, but their **hiring** is uncertain.

steps.text: Record wrong AI answers and reopened complaints for monthly manager meetings
Apply to nearby contact centres if his paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that AGI by 2028 is a direct threat to our calls and chats. I would ask management to say plainly which people they still plan to employ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a sharp cut in our desks by 2028, even if some complaints remain. Robots coming around 2031 do not buy us time because our work is on phones and screens. Four months of savings might carry me through a search, but it would disappear quickly if several centres cut together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager for a written staffing timetable and start saving more from each pay. I would review vacancies at the other centres every week while I still have a wage. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my post ends I would take a paid complaints role elsewhere if one is open; I would move only with an offer that covers rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am alarmed. I can count four months of savings on paper and still picture the money going out through the rent door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you study something new in those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not just because someone says study. If a specific paid job required a short course and the employer covered it, I would consider it; today I would keep the wage and look for openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them I am checking vacancies and have savings, not ask them for money. My parents would help if I truly needed it, but I would rather take paid work first.

say: I would ask management which **posts** remain after AGI.
I would say our screen work faces **2028**, before robots arrive.
think: I could lose four months of **savings** during a shared hiring freeze.
do: Increase my **savings** from each pay while I still have a wage.
feel: My four months feel **short** against rent.
S2.quote: I can count four months of savings on paper and still picture the money going out through the rent door.
fieldNote: He sees the 2028 **thinking-work** threat clearly despite resisting AI tools.
He will consider retraining only for a **specific funded job**.
He prefers paid work to asking his **parents** for help.

steps.text: Save more from each pay before the 2028 arrival
Check paid complaints vacancies weekly; move after job loss only if an offer covers rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets management tell us the truth before the old jobs end. I would ask for a proper staffing timetable rather than a slogan about new opportunities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think our calls could be mostly gone when AGI arrives in 2031. The extra years give me more time to save and watch which nearby centres keep people. I do not want to spend the next five years pretending a new app is a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask for the company forecast in writing and keep building my reserve toward six months of expenses. I would keep my complaint records so I can show another employer what I do well. In the first year after 2031, if the team shrinks I would apply for an actual paid complaints vacancy, including outside town if the wage covers the move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious rather than cornered. I can plan with five years, even if I dislike the direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you attend training if the company offered it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would attend required sessions on paid time. I might take a short funded course for a named complaints role, but I would not enroll now without that opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can your complaint records prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My complaint records show which cases I solved and which customers stayed after the call. A manager at another centre can read my solved-case records more easily than a promise that I am adaptable.

say: I would warn that **old jobs** may end even with five years.
I would say five years allows honest **staffing plans**.
think: I expect calls to shrink by **2031**.
I can build more **savings** while watching real openings at nearby centres.
do: Build a **six-month reserve** and retain case records.
Apply for a paid **complaints vacancy** after 2031 if cut.
S3.quote: A manager at another centre can read my solved-case records more easily than a promise that I am adaptable.
fieldNote: He uses the longer runway for **saving** and evidence of skill.
He rejects vague **retraining** without a named paid role.
An outside-town offer must cover the **move**.

steps.text: Save toward six months of expenses while employed
Apply if the team shrinks; relocate for paid complaints work only if wages cover moving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger agents to learn the account rules thoroughly before worrying about a machine from ten years away. I would also ask management to give people honest dates as the work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be 37 in 2036 and have a stronger reserve by then. I still doubt the calls will stay human once full AGI is here, but I have a decade of wages to prepare. The robots around 2039 matter less to my desk than the earlier thinking software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep leading the complaints team and put a fixed part of each raise into savings. I would watch openings in dispute review and ask what proof of experience those jobs need. In the first year after 2036, if calls disappear I would apply for a paid dispute review post if one exists; I would not resign for a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the end point still changes my work. Ten years leaves me enough time to make sensible choices without racing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on dispute review now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a paid opening came up and they valued my complaint experience, yes. I would not leave the current wage for unpaid shadow work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the decade make you more willing to use AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use a required tool after someone showed me the checks. I am slow with new software. I would rather know the account rules than be first to click a button.

say: I would tell agents to master **account rules**.
I would ask management for honest **change dates** as calls move to software.
think: I can build a stronger **reserve** from a decade of wages before 2036.
My desk faces thinking AI before **robots**.
do: Save a fixed part of each **raise** before spending on anything new.
S4.quote: I would rather know the account rules than be first to click a button.
fieldNote: He remains reluctant to use **AI** voluntarily.
He values verified account skill over being **first** with software.
A paid **opening** remains the condition for moving roles.

steps.text: Keep leading the complaints team while calls remain
Save a fixed part of each pay raise before 2036
Apply for a paid dispute review opening if calls disappear after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A written staffing timetable and real paid openings for complaint specialists would help. Four months of savings gives me a start, but I need to know what job I am looking for.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask who is responsible when the payment record is wrong. Somebody still has to take the call when a machine promises a refund that never arrives, and they need the authority to fix it.

headlineQuote: Somebody still has to take the call when a machine promises a refund that never arrives, and they need the authority to fix it.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old** contact centre lead with a two-year college diploma and typical pay.
He is among the **best agents**, keeps four months of expenses saved, and has some nearby job options.
He has never used **AI** and trusts complaint records and account knowledge more than new tools.
He would save and search for **paid openings** rather than buy vague training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase his desk before nearby centres have room to hire.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing timetable** and actual paid specialist vacancies would give him a usable plan.
